problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =2, & \,{f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to approximate the value of $f(0,2).$

activity_context.topic_title: Second-Degree Taylor Polynomials of Multivariable Functions

examples.knowledge_point: Approximating a Multivariable Function at a Point Using a Quadratic Taylor Polynomial
examples.problem:
For the twice-differentiable function $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R,$ we have the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,0,0) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(1,0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Use the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/32af7a7ab867c247eff15583688e31052e2d640b1be6c6c1b1f8bd19b7b7f2f7.png) to approximate the value of $f(1,1,1).$
examples.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/f27bcd29776525aa543b778627e0aace4e0b0537ceac83f5750a31f5def4f762.png) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/c281563d780c34ea5753498e0e722bfb0296fe06c5d43e82473a45901a1aa7ee.png)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/2fa9abbaad8230a38e1085b8842fbbd970c66addff6f388e13973ee116f0cd37.png)

In this case, we have ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/71175744ceb56efc01b8b18b97d6681b11b8e9b85a1d899fc9a137ab5e3c611c.png) and the following data:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(a) & =-1, & \,{f}^{′}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(a) & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/0d3a22cd82a02ab5122e811236d53eb4c0018e9817d2542163acc005ca5d3764.png)

Finally, evaluating the polynomial at ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070188/assets/dad24b303457c56dc14c11b3b9de6cb827b18b8f3a03059922d1b15521ea119d.png) we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & ≈-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =-1+1+\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
For the function $f:{R}^{2}\to R,$ defined as

$$
f(x,y)={e}^{x+2y},
$$

the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈∗+[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & ∗ \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}∗ \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

Find the sum of the six missing expressions.
feedback.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶z
$$

 

and is twice differentiable at $x=a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
{f}^{′}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]|}_{x=a}
$$

and

$$
{f}^{″}(a)={[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}]}_{x=a}
$$

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0,0) & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2y} & 2{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+2y} & 2{e}^{x+2y} \\ 2{e}^{x+2y} & 4{e}^{x+2y}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(0,0) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial is given by

$$
f(x)≈1+[\begin{aligned}1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]+\frac{1}{2}{[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, the sum of the missing expressions is

$$
1+2+x+x+2+x=3x+5.
$$
